messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Brandt is a 45-year-old widowed military medic of German-Polish descent who presented for psychological assessment following a referral from his unit's medical officer. His PCL-5 score of 66 places him in the severe range for PTSD, and over the course of the intake and early sessions, a coherent and deeply entrenched clinical picture has emerged — one rooted in a natural disaster that stripped him not only of colleagues and patients, but of the framework through which he had understood his life and his purpose.

Eighteen months ago, Aleksander was deployed as part of a disaster relief operation following a catastrophic earthquake in a mountainous region. He had worked as a medic for over two decades and had managed trauma before, but nothing had prepared him for what unfolded over seventy-two hours in a collapsed field hospital. The building came down in an aftershock while he was treating the injured, and in the chaos that followed — the grinding of settling concrete, the screaming that gradually fell silent, the darkness punctuated only by the sounds of people dying — he was unable to reach several patients he had been stabilising. He survived. They did not. He was eventually pulled from the rubble after several hours, disoriented, covered in dust, still holding a tourniquet he did not remember applying.

In the weeks after his evacuation, Aleksander found that the memories of those hours refused to organise themselves into anything coherent. He cannot reconstruct the sequence of events — he cannot say with certainty who he reached first, or when the second aftershock came, or how long he lay still before calling out. The memories arrive not as a narrative but as fragments: the particular grinding sound of shifting debris, the weight of dust in his throat, a hand he held that went slack. When these fragments surface — and they surface often — he does not experience them as recollections. He experiences them as re-immersion. The terror he felt in that rubble returns with the memory intact, and the emotional force of it is so overwhelming that he has had to leave briefings, step away from patients, and on one occasion pull his vehicle over on the highway because he could no longer see clearly through the emotion. He has come to dread the memories themselves, not simply because they are painful, but because he has no way to contain them once they begin.

What has followed from this — and what now forms the gravitational centre of his presentation — is a profound collapse in how Aleksander understands himself and the world. He had built his identity around competence, around the belief that skilled, disciplined action could make a difference in the worst circumstances. The earthquake destroyed that belief at its foundation. He is certain, in a way he cannot argue himself out of, that he failed those patients — that a better medic, a faster medic, would have done more. This appraisal of personal failure and a world stripped of reliable order has become inseparable from the memories themselves: each time the fragments return, they arrive already annotated with the conclusion that he is not who he thought he was, that the world does not work the way he believed, that nothing he does carries meaning anymore. And in the other direction, when he sits with the conviction that his life has lost its purpose, the memories press closer — as though the despair itself opens a door.

His hypervigilance has compounded this picture. At the base where he continues to work, unexpected sounds — a door slamming, a vehicle backfiring in the motor pool, the clatter of equipment — send him into a state of high alert that he cannot readily downregulate. He is unable to relax even in environments he knows to be safe. This sustained physiological arousal has reinforced his sense that something is fundamentally and permanently wrong with him, deepening the conviction that he no longer recognises himself and that the person he was before the earthquake is simply gone.

Occupationally, the consequences have been significant. He has begun avoiding trauma bays and resuscitation scenarios, citing administrative reasons, and a supervising officer has noted his withdrawal from the team. Aleksander is aware of this deterioration. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month when a junior medic asked him for guidance and he found he had nothing to offer — not because he lacked knowledge, but because he no longer believed it mattered. What he most fears is that this is permanent. What he most hopes, though he holds the hope tentatively, is that he might find his way back to someone he can recognise.
